title: Inherited a House That Was Paid-Off? October 2026 Guide
summary: Just inherited a paid-off house? Learn how probate, step-up in basis, and co-ownership with siblings work in this October 2026 guide.
body_markdown:
When someone dies owning a house with no mortgage, that property becomes part of their estate and passes to heirs through a legal process. How that process works depends on how the property was titled and whether it passes through probate. This guide covers the key points for families and heirs to be aware of, including: how probate applies to an inherited house, how to transfer title into your name, what taxes apply, the step-up in basis rule, co-inheriting with siblings, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- A paid-off inherited house still passes through probate unless held in a trust or transfer-on-death deed.
- The step-up in basis resets the cost basis to the date-of-death value,
- Only six states impose inheritance tax; the federal estate tax applies only to estates above $15 million in 2026.
- Elayne searches financial institutions, state unclaimed property registries, and insurance sources to surface accounts and assets connected to the larger estate.


## What Happens When You Inherit a Paid-Off House


Inheriting a paid-off house means the property transfers to you without an outstanding loan attached, but the process is rarely immediate. The house is still an asset of the estate, and before legal ownership reaches you, it typically has to pass through some form of estate administration, which often means probate.


How quickly that happens depends on how the property was titled. A house held in a living trust can transfer within weeks. One that passes through a will, or with no will at all, generally goes through probate court first, which can take months depending on the state. See[property transfer timing after death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-long-do-you-have-to-transfer-property-after-death) for state-specific timing.


During that period, property taxes still come due, the house needs insurance, and if there are other heirs, decisions about the property cannot be made unilaterally.

## The Probate Process for an Inherited House


Probate is the court-supervised process of validating a will, appointing someone to manage the estate, and overseeing how assets including real property transfer to the right people. For a house, it means the court confirms who has authority to act, creditors get notified, and title transfers once the proceeding closes.


Not every inherited house goes through probate, since a house can fall on either side of[probate vs. non-probate assets](https://www.elayne.com/resources/probate-vs-non-probate-assets) . Property held in a living trust, titled with a transfer-on-death deed, or owned as joint tenancy with right of survivorship passes outside probate entirely. In those cases, title transfers through a simpler legal mechanism without court involvement.


When probate is required, timelines vary widely by state. Some states have simplified processes for smaller estates; others move slowly. During that window, the executor manages the property but cannot sell or transfer it without court authority. If there is no will, the court appoints an administrator and distributes the estate according to state intestacy laws. See[real estate without a will](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-happens-to-real-estate-without-a-will) for more details.


## Putting an Inherited House in Your Name


Getting the house into your name requires authority to act, and a recorded deed.


If the house went through probate, the court issues Letters Testamentary to[the executor](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/information-for-executors) . That document grants authority to transfer the property. The executor prepares a new deed conveying title to the heir, which is then recorded with the county recorder's office where the property sits. The recording is typically completed within days once the deed is filed.


If the house passed outside probate through a trust or[transfer on death deed](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-is-a-transfer-on-death-deed-how-tod-deeds-help-you-skip-probate) , a small estate affidavit may suffice in place of court-issued letters, depending on the state.


Once title is recorded, two additional items typically follow:


- Updating homeowner's insurance to reflect the new owner, so coverage does not lapse during the transition
- Notifying the county assessor's office so property tax records reflect the change and billing reaches the right person


## Taxes on an Inherited House


Separate taxes can apply to an inherited house, and they work differently.


Federal estate tax is paid by the estate, not by the heir. In 2026, it[applies to estates above $15 million](https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/personal-finance/what-is-the-estate-tax-exemption) . A small number of states impose their own estate taxes with lower thresholds, meaning a state bill is possible even when no federal tax is owed.


The step-up in basis is the most consequential tax rule for many heirs, and it shapes[how inherited property is taxed when sold](https://www.elayne.com/resources/taxes-on-selling-inherited-property) . When you inherit a house, your cost basis resets to the property's fair market value on the date of death. If the home was bought for $100,000 and is worth $400,000 when you inherit it, your basis becomes $400,000, and any taxable gain only begins from that point forward.


## Inheriting a House With Siblings


When multiple siblings inherit a house together, they become co-owners the moment title transfers. How that co-ownership is structured determines what each person can do with their share.


### Tenancy in Common vs. Joint Tenancy


The distinction between[joint tenancy and tenancy in common](https://www.elayne.com/resources/joint-tenancy-tenants-in-common-executors) matters here: tenancy in common means each sibling holds a separate, transferable interest. One sibling can sell or mortgage their share without the others' consent, and shares need not be equal. Joint tenancy includes a[right of survivorship](https://www.elayne.com/resources/right-of-survivorship-wills-taxes-property) , so when one co-owner dies, their share passes automatically to the remaining owners instead of through their estate.

## FAQ


### How do I put an inherited house in my name after probate?


Once probate closes, the executor uses court-issued Letters Testamentary to prepare a new deed conveying title to the heir, which is then recorded with the county recorder's office where the property sits. If the house passed outside probate through a trust or transfer-on-death deed, a small estate affidavit may suffice depending on the state. After recording, homeowner's insurance is updated to reflect the new owner and the county assessor's office is notified so property tax billing reaches the correct party.


### Inheriting a house with siblings: what happens when one sibling refuses to sell or leave?


Any co-owner can file a partition action, which allows a court to compel either a physical division or a forced sale regardless of whether the occupying sibling agrees. Before filing, many estate attorneys recommend documenting negotiation attempts in writing, requesting a formal accounting of rental value and shared expenses, and confirming whether an ouster claim applies under your state's law.


### What is probate for a house, and when is it required?


Probate is the court-supervised process of validating a will, appointing someone to manage the estate, and overseeing how assets including real property transfer to the right people. Not every inherited house goes through probate: property held in a living trust, titled with a transfer-on-death deed, or owned as joint tenancy with right of survivorship passes outside probate entirely through a simpler legal mechanism. When probate is required, the executor manages the property during the proceeding but cannot sell or transfer it without court authority, and timelines vary by state.


### What is the step-up in basis, and how does it apply to an inherited house?


When a house is inherited, the heir's cost basis resets to the property's fair market value on the date of death. This is called the step-up in basis. If the original owner paid $120,000 for the home and it is worth $450,000 at the time of death, the heir's basis becomes $450,000. Any taxable capital gain is calculated only from that new, higher starting point, not from the original purchase price. This rule often significantly reduces the capital gains tax owed if the heir sells the property.


### Who pays property taxes on an inherited house during probate?


Property taxes continue to accrue during probate and are treated as an estate expense. The executor is responsible for paying them from estate funds while the proceeding is open. If the property passes outside probate through a trust or transfer-on-death deed, the heir becomes responsible for property taxes as soon as title transfers. Unpaid property taxes can lead to liens against the property, so keeping them current during the transition period is part of routine estate administration.


### Can an heir rent out an inherited house before selling it?


Whether an heir can rent out the property depends on the stage of administration. During probate, the executor may be able to rent the property to cover carrying costs, but this typically requires court authorization and must be handled as an estate matter. Once title transfers to the heir, that person holds full ownership rights and can rent the property under standard landlord rules. Rental income received after the heir takes title is treated as ordinary income for tax purposes.
